verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign. He reigned eleven years in Jerusalem: and his mother’s name was Hamutal the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.
For through Yahweh’s anger this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out from his presence. Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came, he and all his army, against Jerusalem, and encamped against it; and they built forts against it round about.
So the city was besieged to the eleventh year of king Zedekiah.
In the fourth month, in the ninth day of the month, the famine was severe in the city, so that there was no bread for the people of the land.

Then a breach was made in the city, and all the men of war fled, and went out of the city by night by the way of the gate between the two walls, which was by the king’s garden. Now the Chaldeans were against the city all around. The men of war went toward the Arabah,
but the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; and all his army was scattered from him.
Then they took the king, and carried him up to the king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; and he gave judgment on him.
The king of Babylon killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes: he killed also all the princes of Judah in Riblah.
He put out the eyes of Zedekiah; and the king of Babylon bound him in fetters, and carried him to Babylon, and put him in prison until the day of his death.

Now in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month, which was the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, who stood before the king of Babylon, came into Jerusalem.
He burned Yahweh’s house, and the king’s house; and all the houses of Jerusalem, even every great house, he burned with fire.
All the army of the Chaldeans, who were with the captain of the guard, broke down all the walls of Jerusalem all around.

Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the poorest of the people, and the residue of the people who were left in the city, and those who fell away, who fell to the king of Babylon, and the residue of the multitude.
But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poorest of the land to be vineyard keepers and farmers.
The Chaldeans broke the pillars of brass that were in Yahweh’s house, and the bases and the bronze sea that were in Yahweh’s house in pieces, and carried all of their brass to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and all the vessels of brass with which they ministered.
The captain of the guard took away the cups, the fire pans, the basins, the pots, the lamp stands, the spoons, and the bowls; that which was of gold, in gold, and that which was of silver, in silver.
They took the two pillars, the one sea, and the twelve bronze bulls that were under the bases, which king Solomon had made for Yahweh’s house. The brass of all these vessels was without weight.
As for the pillars, the height of the one pillar was eighteen cubits;  and a line of twelve cubits encircled it; and its thickness was four fingers. It was hollow.

A capital of brass was on it; and the height of the one capital was five cubits,  with network and pomegranates on the capital all around, all of brass: and the second pillar also had like these, and pomegranates.
There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; all the pomegranates were one hundred on the network all around.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold:

and out of the city he took an officer who was set over the men of war; and seven men of those who saw the king’s face, who were found in the city; and the scribe of the captain of the army, who mustered the people of the land; and sixty men of the people of the land, who were found in the middle of the city.
Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them, and brought them to the king of Babylon to Riblah.
The king of Babylon struck them, and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land.
This is the people whom Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive: in the seventh year three thousand twenty-three Jews;
in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar he carried away captive from Jerusalem eight hundred thirty-two persons;
in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive of the Jews seven hundred forty-five persons: all the persons were four thousand and six hundred.

In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, in the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evilmerodach king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and released him from prison;
and he spoke kindly to him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings who were with him in Babylon,
and changed his prison garments. Jehoiachin ate bread before him continually all the days of his life:
and for his allowance, there was a continual allowance given him by the king of Babylon, every day a portion until the day of his death, all the days of his life.

footnotes.content: Zedekiah begins his reign at twenty-one—young, untested, with a mother from Libnah behind him. Youth and good lineage don't guarantee faithfulness. I've watched many young hearts set out with every advantage and still stumble when they don't anchor themselves to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did evil 'according to all that Jehoiakim had done'—he copied the worst from his predecessor, not the best. How quickly we can inherit a bad example and call it tradition. The Lord sees when we choose the crooked path instead of turning toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's anger is not petty; it's the Holy One turning away because His people have turned away. When Zedekiah rebels against Babylon's king, he rebels first against the Lord who could have protected him. Judgment always comes when we harden our hearts against grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the ninth year, on that tenth day of the tenth month—history marks its turning point with terrible precision. Nebuchadnezzar comes with all his army, and the walls begin to close in. The Lord had warned them through the prophets; now the walls speak louder than any voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two years of siege—the city starved while the king waited for a rescue that never came. Long suffering has a way of breaking what pride had armored. Yet even in captivity's approach, there is still a moment where repentance might yet turn the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Famine in the ninth day of the fourth month—no bread for the people. When we refuse to bend, we bend those under us into hunger and despair. A leader's stubbornness becomes his people's agony. The Lord grieves over such hardness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A breach in the city wall, soldiers fleeing by night through the gate between two walls and the king's garden—the exact route of escape. The gate between walls is narrow escape; the king's garden, once a place of abundance, now a route to flight. Even the once-beautiful places speak of ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They overtook him in the plains of Jericho, and his army scattered. There is no escape from the Lord's judgment once a leader has despised His word. The plains of Jericho—where Joshua once saw the walls fall at God's command—now witness a king brought low.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They carried him to Riblah in the land of Hamath, where the Babylonian king 'gave judgment on him.' That phrase is terrible in its calm—like a sentence already written before the hearing. Zedekiah's rebellion ends not in glory but in the courtroom of a foreign king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His sons killed before his eyes—then all the princes of Judah. The cruelty is calculated: let the king watch what his choices have wrought. I grieve that Judah's leaders paid the price for refusing to listen when the Lord sent them prophets year after year.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They put out Zedekiah's eyes, bound him in fetters, and locked him in prison until he died. Darkness in body mirrors the spiritual blindness he chose when he turned from the Lord. Yet even there, in prison, he lived on—not destroyed, but broken, a living reminder of what rebellion brings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year, on the tenth day, Nebuzaradan the captain came into Jerusalem. That date marks when the destruction truly began—methodical, arranged, final. The Lord's judgment was not wild but ordered, as if a doorway was closing behind them forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He burned the house of Yahweh—the Temple, holy and set apart. He burned the king's house and every great house with fire. The most sacred and the mightiest fell alike. I think of how long it had taken to build those walls, and how quickly the flame consumed them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the walls of Jerusalem came down all around—completely. There was no corner of safety, no height left to defend. The people who once said, 'The Temple of the Lord, the Temple of the Lord' trusted in walls instead of in His mercy. The walls fell.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poorest were carried away—those who had nothing to offer, the residue left in the city. War has a way of taking even the least. Yet the Lord sees every captive, and even in Babylon, His eye will not leave them. The exile is not the end of His story.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Of the poorest, some were left behind to be vineyard keepers and farmers. The Lord left remnants—those who would work the land, tend the vines, keep the soil alive. Even in judgment, there is seed. Even in captivity, some remain to remember and to tend.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The bronze pillars, the bases, the sea—all the brass of Yahweh's house was broken into pieces and carried to Babylon. These were Solomon's great works, intricate and beautiful. But brass can be melted and recast; the Lord's faithfulness cannot be taken captive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pots, shovels, snuffers, basins, spoons—all the vessels that served in the Temple were taken. Such specific detail saddens me: even the smallest tools of worship were stripped away. The Lord does not forget these small sacraments, and neither do those who loved them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cups, fire pans, basins, pots, lamp stands, spoons, bowls—gold and silver sorted carefully. Even in plunder, there is order; even in robbery, there is accounting. The Babylonians were meticulous, but they could not plunder what mattered most: the covenant, the memory, the seed of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The two pillars, the sea, and the twelve bronze bulls that Solomon made—all the brass was 'without weight,' too great to measure. These are real things, crafted by the greatest hands Judah had ever known. Yet all such work, no matter how glorious, yields to the Lord's hand when a people will not turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eighteen cubits high, twelve cubits around, four fingers thick, hollow inside—the pillar is measured and described, reduced to its dimensions. A heart can be mighty to behold and yet hollow when it has turned from the Lord. These pillars stand as testament to that tragedy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A capital of brass five cubits high, with network and pomegranates all around—such beauty and craft. The pomegranate is a sign of abundance and life; even in the pillars that would be broken, there was promise woven in. The Lord loved His people's beauty, and it grieves Him to see it fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ninety-six pomegranates on the sides, one hundred all around the network—such particularity in the fruitfulness carved there. The Lord delighted in this abundance that His people crafted to honor Him. I see in those pomegranates the abundance that could have remained if they had only turned their hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and three keepers of the threshold—the officers of the Temple were led away captive. Those who stood in the most sacred place, who knew the holiness of the sanctuary, now go into exile. Their captivity speaks loudest to what has been lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An officer of the men of war, seven men who saw the king's face, the scribe, and sixty common men—the leadership and the people together. All ranks fell into captivity. There is no protection in rank, no safety in proximity to power, when a nation turns from the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nebuzaradan brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. Each person, each name lost to us now, was transported from the land of their fathers to serve in a strange land. Yet the Lord was not absent from Riblah; He goes into exile with His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king of Babylon struck them and put them to death in Hamath. So Judah was carried away captive out of his land. The sentence is complete, the exile begins. Yet I know what the Lord whispered through Jeremiah to those same exiles: even in Babylon, build houses, plant gardens, seek the peace of the city.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the seventh year, three thousand twenty-three Jews were carried captive. The numbering begins—a careful accounting of loss. Each number represents a family, a story, a heart grieving for Jerusalem. The Lord numbers them all and holds each one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the eighteenth year, eight hundred thirty-two more were taken. The captivities come in waves, each year another removal. Exile is not a single terrible moment but a long, grinding loss. Yet each wave still carries the Lord's people toward a day of restoration.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the twenty-third year, seven hundred forty-five more—all the persons numbered were four thousand and six hundred. These numbers add to a people, scattered but counted, displaced but known. The Lord does not lose even one in the multitude of exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the thirty-seventh year of captivity—thirty-seven years in a strange land—Evilmerodach lifted up the head of Jehoiachin and released him from prison. A king born into exile hears one day that he is no longer bound. After so long, mercy finds him like dawn after the longest night.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Evilmerodach spoke kindly to him and set his throne above the thrones of other captive kings. Kindness, when it comes after such long cruelty, feels almost like it bends time itself. The Lord had not forgotten His mercy; He set it in the heart of a Babylonian king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiachin's prison garments were changed; he ate bread before the king continually. He was no longer a prisoner but a guest, though still far from home. The change of clothes, the place at the table—small graces that taste like hope when you have forgotten what hope was.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A continual allowance given to him every day until the day of his death—after thirty-seven years, provision became his daily bread. Readers today hear an echo in this: the Lord gives us daily bread, daily mercy, day after day, whether in exile or at home. Our Redeemer provides when we cannot provide for ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
